newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian media says problems with U.S. remain.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian media says problems with U.S. remain.

text.p: Indonesia reacted warmly to U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election but news reports and editorials on Thursday said problems in Indonesian-U.S. relations were not going to disappear overnight.

The Jakarta Post newspaper said in an editorial that it did not see the issue of controversial funding of the Democratic Party by an Indonesian businessman as fading away simply because the elections were over.

"We have certainly not heard the last of what has been dubbed by the American press during the campaign as the 'Riady Connection', so-named after the Indonesian businessman who contributed huge sums of money to Clinton's election coffers," the paper said.
Republicans during the election campaign raised the question of donations to the Democrats by people connected to Indonesia's Lippo group, headed by the wealthy Riady family.

The editorial said Clinton's re-election gave continuity to Indonesian-American relations but added that the American president was likely to get tougher on a number of issues now he was firmly back in power.
"Clinton, no longer inhibited by re-election worries, is bound to be more assertive and will stand more firmly on his principles," the paper said.
"On Indonesia-U.S. relations this means he will likely be more firm on the question of human rights and East Timor, two issues that have gotten in the way of our relations."

Harian Ekonomi Neraca quoted Raja Silalahi, an economic analyst at the Indonesian Centre for Strategic International Studies (CSIS), as also saying Clinton was likely to push American interests more firmly than during his first term.
Raja said the United States had become more critical of Indonesia recently on a number of matters.

"America is critical of Indonesia on the national car programme, environmental issues, human rights issues and product dumping," Raja said, adding that these problems rose out of a misunderstanding of Asia.

The United States, Japan and the European Union have all complained to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over Indonesia's national car policy which they say breaks international free trade regulations by giving tariff and tax breaks to only one firm.
Kompas newspaper said Clinton's victory on a platform of compassion gave hope to people around the world.
"The voters showed their belief in Clinton once again because of economic performance and the compassion that they see in him," it said in an editorial.
